notes: Garden Tracker Preserve & Store pack. Processing times are parsed from NCHFP (USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning) pages — never typed by hand. Published remotely at GT_CONFIG.STORAGE_DATA_URL.

l1: Only use tested recipes. A tested recipe was checked in a lab so the jar is safe.
Vegetables, beans and corn are “low-acid.” They MUST go in a pressure canner. A pot of boiling water is not hot enough for them.
If a lid bulges, leaks, spurts, smells bad or has mold, do not taste it. Throw it out the safe way.
l2: Botulism is a rare but deadly food poisoning. Its germs (spores) are on most fresh food, live without air, and make poison inside sealed jars of low-acid food.
Acid stops them. Most fruits are acid enough for a boiling-water canner. Tomatoes are borderline, so tested tomato recipes add lemon juice or citric acid.
Never invent your own times or change a recipe’s amounts, jar size or method. If a time is not from USDA or NCHFP, Garden Tracker will not show one.
l3: Low-acid foods have a pH above 4.6 — all fresh vegetables except most tomatoes. Mixtures of low-acid and acid foods are usually low-acid too, unless the tested recipe adds enough acid.
Not recommended (unsafe): open-kettle canning, oven canning, microwave or dishwasher “canning,” and “dry canning.” Steam canners are only for acid foods, and only with the tested directions.
Store sealed jars below 95°F; 50–70°F keeps the best quality. Use home-canned food within a year.
mistakes: Using a recipe from a blog, an old cookbook or a relative without checking it is tested.
Water-bath canning green beans, corn or other vegetables.
Tasting a jar to see if it is OK.
Adding extra onions, peppers or thickeners to a tested salsa or sauce.

l1: Boiling-water canning is for high-acid foods: fruit, jam, pickles, and tomatoes with lemon juice added.
Jars sit on a rack in a big pot, covered by boiling water, for the time the tested recipe says.
l2: Start timing only when the water is boiling hard. If it stops boiling, bring it back to a boil and start the time over.
Live high up? Water boils at a lower temperature, so tested recipes add minutes. Garden Tracker uses your garden’s elevation to point at the right row.
l3: Water must be at least 1 inch over the jar tops — 2 inches for processes over 30 minutes. Preheat to 140°F for raw-packed and 180°F for hot-packed food.
After processing: heat off, lid off, wait 5 minutes, lift jars out upright and cool 12 to 24 hours without touching. Then check seals.
Jams, jellies and pickles processed less than 10 minutes go in sterilized jars.
equip: Boiling-water canner (or deep pot) with a rack and lid
NEW two-piece lids (bands can be reused)
Bottled lemon juice or citric acid (tomatoes)
steps: Pick a tested recipe (USDA, NCHFP or your extension office).
Wash jars, lids and bands in hot soapy water. Keep jars hot.
Put the rack in the canner, fill halfway with water and heat it.
Prepare the food exactly as the recipe says.
Fill jars, leaving the headspace the recipe lists.
Remove air bubbles, wipe the rims, put on lids and bands fingertip-tight.
Lower jars into the canner; add hot water to cover by 1 inch (2 inches for long processes).
Bring to a full boil, cover, and start the timer (use your elevation’s time).
Heat off, lid off, wait 5 minutes, lift jars out straight up.
Cool 12–24 hours, check seals, label with date, store cool and dark.
mistakes: Starting the timer before the water boils hard.
Tightening bands too hard (air cannot escape).

l1: Low-acid foods — green beans, corn, peas, carrots, potatoes, beets, greens, squash cubes — must be pressure canned.
A pressure canner gets hotter than boiling water. That heat is what kills botulism spores.
l2: Pressure itself does not kill germs — the high temperature does. Air trapped inside lowers the temperature, so every canner is vented (steam pours out) for 10 minutes before you close it.
Higher elevation means lower temperature, so you use more pressure. Garden Tracker reads your elevation and highlights your pressure.
Dial gauges must be checked for accuracy every year — many county extension offices test them.
l3: At sea level, 10.5 lb on a gauge gives 240°F inside. Dial-gauge tables step up the pressure with elevation; weighted-gauge canners go from 10 to 15 lb above 1,000 feet.
If pressure drops below the target at any time, bring it back up and restart the whole time.
Never force-cool. Let it drop to zero on its own, remove the weight, wait 10 minutes, then open the lid away from your face.
Mayonnaise-type jars break in pressure canners — use real canning jars. Pressure saucepans (small cookers) are not recommended.
equip: Pressure CANNER (not a small pressure cooker) with rack
Dial gauge tested this year, or a weighted gauge
Good lid gasket and clear vent pipe
Mason-type canning jars and NEW lids
The tested NCHFP/USDA directions for the food
steps: Check the canner: clean gasket, clear vent pipe, gauge tested this year.
Put the rack and 2–3 inches of hot water in the canner (or what the directions say).
Fill hot jars with the food, leaving the listed headspace. Wipe rims; put on lids.
Load jars on the rack and lock the lid. Leave the weight off.
Heat on high until steam pours out. Vent 10 minutes.
Put on the weight (or close the petcock). Let pressure rise.
Start timing when your pressure is reached. Keep it steady; restart if it drops.
Heat off. Let pressure fall to zero by itself — never cool it with water.
Remove the weight, wait 10 minutes, open the lid away from you.
Lift jars out upright; cool 12–24 hours; check seals; label and store.
mistakes: Opening the canner early or cooling it with water.
Canning mashed pumpkin or squash (no tested process — can cubes only).

quiz.q: Why vent the canner for 10 minutes?
a: To push out air so it gets hot enough

l1: Freezing is the easiest way to keep vegetables. Most need a quick dip in boiling water first — called blanching.
Blanching stops the vegetable from losing color, taste and vitamins in the freezer. Then cool it fast in ice water.
l2: Blanching time depends on the vegetable and the size of the pieces. Each crop’s “Storing it” card shows its NCHFP time.
Too short is worse than none — it wakes enzymes up. Too long cooks it soft.
Freeze at 0°F or colder. Most frozen fruits and vegetables keep their best quality 8 to 12 months.
l3: Use 1 gallon of water per pound of vegetables. Start timing when the water comes back to a boil. Cool in ice water for the same time you blanched.
Lettuce, radishes, cress and raw cabbage or cucumbers (except as pickles or slaw-type recipes) do not freeze well.
equip: Large pot with a lid and a blanching basket
steps: Wash, trim and cut the vegetable.
Bring a gallon of water per pound to a rolling boil.
Put the vegetable in; time from when it boils again (see the crop’s NCHFP time).
Move it straight into ice water for the same time.
Drain well and pat dry.
Pack in bags, squeeze out air, leave a little room to expand.
Label with crop and date; freeze flat at 0°F.
mistakes: Skipping blanching on vegetables that need it.
Packing warm food into the freezer.
Freezing too much at once so it freezes slowly.

l1: Drying takes the water out so germs cannot grow. Herbs, hot peppers, beans and popcorn dry well.
A food dehydrator is the easiest way. Dried food goes in tight jars, somewhere cool, dry and dark.
l2: Dehydrators are made to dry food fast at 140°F. Herbs dry at a lower temperature (95–115°F) to keep their oils.
Fruits can be sun-dried on hot, dry, breezy days. Vegetables should be dried indoors (vine-dried beans are the exception) because they are low in sugar and acid.
Dried food keeps 4 months to 1 year. Fruits keep about 1 year at 60°F but only 6 months at 80°F; vegetables keep about half as long.
l3: Cool food completely before packing — warm food sweats and can mold. Pack in amounts you will use at once.
Glass jars let you see moisture. If drops appear, the food was not dry enough — dry it again or use it now.
Vine-dried beans: after harvest, freeze them or heat them in a 160°F oven for 30 minutes to kill insect eggs before storing.
equip: Clean, dry glass jars or freezer bags
Paper bags and string (for hanging herbs)
steps: Pick fresh, ripe, clean produce.
Cut into even, thin pieces so they dry at the same speed.
Blanch or pretreat if the crop’s NCHFP directions say so.
Spread in one layer with space for air.
Dry until leathery or crisp (herbs crumble).
Cool completely.
Pack tight in jars; check for moisture the first week; label and date.
mistakes: Storing in a warm, bright spot.

l1: Pickles use vinegar or salt to make food sour, which keeps it safe.
Fermenting (like sauerkraut) lets good bacteria make the sour taste over a few weeks.
l2: Use only tested pickle recipes and never cut back the vinegar, salt or acid. Use canning or pickling salt.
Sauerkraut ferments in 3 to 4 weeks at 70–75°F, or 5 to 6 weeks at 60–65°F. Above 75°F it can go soft.
Fermented dill pickles: 70–75°F for about 3 to 4 weeks. If pickles get soft, slimy or smell bad, throw them out.
l3: Fully fermented pickles keep about 4 to 6 months in the refrigerator if scum and mold are removed. For the shelf, process them in a boiling-water canner with the tested directions.
Quick fridge pickles are not canned — keep them refrigerated.
Weigh down fermenting food under the brine with a brine-filled bag or plate so no food touches air.
equip: Food-grade crock, glass jar or plastic container (fermenting)
Boiling-water canner, jars and new lids (shelf pickles)
steps: Choose a tested pickle or kraut recipe.
Use fresh, firm, unwaxed produce (pickle cucumbers within 24 hours of picking).
Measure salt, vinegar and water exactly.
Pack and cover with brine; weigh the food under the brine.
Ferment at the listed temperature, checking a few times a week; skim scum.
Refrigerate, or can using the tested boiling-water directions.
mistakes: Using table salt with additives or the wrong vinegar strength.
Cutting back the vinegar or salt.
Letting food poke out above the brine.

quiz.q: What should you do with soft, slimy, bad-smelling pickles?

l1: Some crops keep for months without a fridge: potatoes, carrots, beets, onions, winter squash.
Each crop likes its own spot. Carrots like it cold and damp. Onions like it cool and dry. Squash and sweet potatoes like it warmer.
l2: Only store your best: mature, dry, no cuts or bruises. One rotting potato can spoil the bin — check every week or two.
Cold and moist (carrots, beets, turnips, parsnips): pack in damp sand, sawdust or perforated bags in a basement corner or garage that stays above freezing.
Cool and dry (onions, garlic): mesh bags or braids where air moves. Warm and dry (winter squash, pumpkins, sweet potatoes): a closet or spare room.
l3: Do not store potatoes with apples or other fruit — ripening fruit gives off ethylene gas, which makes the tubers sprout.
Potatoes in the light turn green; the green parts are bitter and should be cut off.
The “Storing it” card for each crop shows the temperature, humidity and months from extension tables. Use those, then watch your own spot with a thermometer.
equip: Thermometer (and a humidity meter if you can)
Old blankets to cover on the coldest nights
steps: Harvest in dry weather; brush off soil (do not wash roots for storage).
Cure crops that need it first (see Curing).
Sort: store only perfect ones; eat the bruised first.
Trim carrot and beet tops to about 1 inch.
Pack each crop where its temperature and humidity fit.
Check every week or two; remove anything soft.

l1: Curing means letting some crops rest before storing, so their skins get tough and they keep longer.
Onions, garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes and winter squash all need curing.
l2: Potatoes: cool, humid and dark for about two weeks so small cuts heal.
Sweet potatoes: warm and humid — at home, a warm shady spot for 10–14 days.
Onions and garlic: warm, dry and airy until the necks are dry and skins rustle. Winter squash (not acorn): warm for about 10 days.
l3: Each crop’s “Storing it” card shows its sourced curing temperature, humidity and days.
Handle gently — bruises do not heal.
Never cure or store sweet potatoes below 55°F.
steps: Harvest on a dry day.
Handle gently; do not wash.
Spread in one layer where the crop’s curing conditions fit.
Cure the listed days.
Trim (onion and garlic tops), sort out damaged ones.
Move to long-term storage.
mistakes: Curing in sun (potatoes turn green, onions scald).

a: So small cuts heal and they keep longer

l1: You can save seeds from your best plants to grow next year.
Tomatoes, peppers, beans and peas are the easiest. Pick “open-pollinated” or heirloom kinds — seeds from hybrids do not grow the same.
l2: Tomato seeds: scoop seeds and gel into a jar with water, swirl twice a day; they sink in about five days. Rinse and dry.
Beans and peas: leave pods on the plant until dry and rattling, then dry indoors at least two weeks.
Keep seeds dry and cool — 32 to 41°F is ideal, so the fridge works. Label and use within one year.
l3: Corn, squash, melons and cucumbers cross with neighbors, so their seeds may not come true.

Cold stratification: some seeds (many trees and wildflowers) need a cold, moist rest before they sprout. Mix them with damp sand or peat in a bag in the fridge; many tree seeds need 32–40°F for 3 to 4 months.
Use the time on the seed packet or a species guide when you have one.
equip: Silica gel or powdered milk in tissue (desiccant)
Paper towels or screens for drying
steps: Choose healthy, open-pollinated plants with the best fruit.
Let fruit or pods ripen fully.
Clean the seeds (ferment tomato seeds).
Dry them completely.
Seal in labeled jars with a desiccant; keep cool.
For stratification, start the cold, moist treatment in time to plant.
mistakes: Saving seed from hybrids and expecting the same plant.
Saving squash seed when other squash grew nearby.

signs: Lid bulging, swollen or not sealed
Streaks of dried food from the top of the jar
Mold, or an off or unnatural smell
steps: Do not open, taste or smell to test it. Never feed it to pets.
Treat any suspect low-acid or tomato product as if it has botulism toxin.
Still sealed: put the jar in a heavy garbage bag, close it, and put it in the regular trash (not the compost).
Leaking or unsealed: follow the NCHFP detoxification steps (boil 30 minutes, covered) before throwing it away — or call your extension office.
Clean every surface it touched with 1 part bleach to 5 parts water; let it stand 30 minutes. Wear gloves. Wash hands well.

seals.text: Unsealed after 24 hours? Reprocess within 24 hours with a new lid, or refrigerate and eat within several days. Remove bands before storing, wash jars, label with contents and date.

vg483.d: Victory gardeners stored carrots, beets, turnips and potatoes in a cool, moist cellar where they would not freeze; onions “cool, dry … preferably about 35° F”; sweet potatoes at 55°–60° F; winter squash at 50°–60° F. Surplus beans and peas were ripened, threshed, dried and kept in closed containers. Today’s extension numbers above are the ones to follow.

vg-leaders.d: Neighbors held community canning days “like a sewing bee,” rented space in quick-freezing lockers, and dried food because it needed no sugar, rubber rings or metal caps. Even then the handbook warned: can no vegetables except tomatoes without a pressure cooker. Times and methods from the 1940s are NOT used today — follow the current USDA guide.

vg-1942.d: The 1942 manual described a partitioned, insulated cellar room with a window for air, roots packed in sand, and outdoor barrel pits for winter storage — all kept cold, steady and just above freezing.

vg-store1943.t: 1943 · USDA “Now to store your canned garden”
vg-store1943.d: Wartime extension agents told families to brace their shelves for the weight of a season’s jars, use adjustable shelves to fit more pints and quarts, and keep canned food in its own cool, ventilated pantry — apart from the bins of root vegetables.

vg-freeze1944.t: 1944 · USDA “Freezing vegetables and fruit from your garden”
vg-freeze1944.d: Families rented freezer lockers in town. The advice then is still good today: freeze produce at its prime, the same day it is picked, and blanch vegetables first.
